stem: A 58-year-old man spent 25 years sandblasting and now has slowly worsening breathlessness. Chest x-ray shows many small rounded nodules, and the hilar lymph nodes have thin rims of calcification like eggshells.
oneliner: 58M + 25 years sandblasting + small rounded nodules + eggshell calcification of hilar nodes → which lung zone?
ask: Which part of the lung is most heavily involved?

options.C: Diffuse uniform involvement of all lobes
options.D: Upper lobes, mainly the posterior zones
options.E: Perihilar lower zones in a bat-wing pattern

whyNot.A: Basal subpleural fibrosis is **asbestosis** (shipyard-type exposure), not the **eggshell-calcified nodules** of sandblasting
whyNot.B: Middle lobe and lingula involvement suggests **bronchiectasis or middle lobe syndrome**, not a dust nodule pattern
whyNot.C: Dust nodules are **zonal**, concentrated in one region, not spread **uniformly**
whyNot.E: A perihilar **bat-wing** pattern means **pulmonary edema**, not calcified nodules

why: Sandblasting exposes workers to silica, and **small nodules with eggshell calcification** of hilar nodes mean **silicosis**. Silicosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis favor the **upper lobes**, whereas **asbestosis** favors the lower lobes.

idea.rule: Silica and coal dust pneumoconioses sit in the upper lobes; asbestosis sits in the lower lobes.
also: Silicosis raises tuberculosis risk by impairing macrophage function
Berylliosis also favors the upper lobes
Asbestosis shows basal fibrosis, pleural plaques and ferruginous bodies
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis forms coal macules and nodules in the upper zones

stem: A 70-year-old man with alcohol use disorder was found drowsy in an armchair after a binge. Five days later he has fever, cough and foul-smelling sputum, and chest x-ray shows a cavity with an air-fluid level.
oneliner: 70M + alcohol use + drowsy while sitting upright + fever and foul sputum 5 days later + cavity with air-fluid level → which lobe?
ask: In which part of the lung is this lesion most likely located?

whyNot.A: The **right** main bronchus is wider and straighter, so aspirated material goes to the right more often than the left
whyNot.B: He was **sitting**; the right middle lobe is not the dependent area in an upright patient
whyNot.D: The lingula is not dependent in an **upright** position, and the left bronchus is less direct
whyNot.E: The apex is the **least dependent** area; material does not travel upward to it in a sitting patient

answer: Right lower lobe (basal segments): aspiration lung abscess
why: Alcohol dulls consciousness and the gag reflex, so mouth flora with **anaerobes** are aspirated. Material follows gravity and the **wider, more vertical right main bronchus**: in an **upright** patient it reaches the **basal segments of the right lower lobe**. The **foul sputum and cavity** fit an anaerobic lung abscess.

idea.rule: Upright aspiration lands in the basal right lower lobe; supine aspiration lands in the posterior right upper lobe or superior right lower segment.
also: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
Aspiration abscess is caused by mouth anaerobes such as Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium and Bacteroides
Risk factors: alcohol, seizures, stroke and swallowing disorders
A supine patient aspirates into the superior segment of the right lower lobe

stem: A 34-year-old construction worker has had fever, cough and tender red nodules on both shins for two weeks, beginning soon after digging in dry ground during a dust storm. Lung biopsy shows large spherules packed with small endospores, and complement-fixing antibody is positive.
oneliner: 34M + construction worker + dust exposure + fever, cough and shin nodules + spherules with endospores → which endemic region?
ask: In which region is the causative organism endemic?

options.A: Desert Southwest and San Joaquin Valley
options.C: Great Lakes and the upper Midwest

whyNot.B: That region is home to **Histoplasma** (small yeasts inside macrophages), not **spherules with endospores**
whyNot.C: That region is home to **Blastomyces** (broad-based budding yeast), not **spherules**
whyNot.D: **Blastomyces** also occurs in the Southeast, but it forms **budding yeast**, not **spherules**
whyNot.E: No dimorphic fungus is tied to these woodlands; they are known for **tick-borne disease**, not **spherules**

answer: Southwestern US deserts and California's San Joaquin Valley (Coccidioides)
why: **Spherules with endospores** identify **Coccidioides**, which lives in desert soil and is inhaled in **dust** from digging or dust storms. **Erythema nodosum** is a common hypersensitivity sign. The fungus is endemic to the **desert Southwest** and California's **San Joaquin Valley**.

idea.rule: Coccidioides = desert Southwest and San Joaquin Valley; Histoplasma = Ohio/Mississippi valleys; Blastomyces = east-central US and Great Lakes.
also: Coccidioides forms spherules with endospores in tissue; Histoplasma forms small yeasts inside macrophages
Blastomyces is a broad-based budding yeast causing skin and bone lesions
Coccidioides can disseminate, with higher risk in pregnancy and in Filipino and African American patients
Erythema nodosum with fever and cough after desert travel suggests coccidioidomycosis

stem: A 72-year-old woman has a mass in the posterior mediastinum removed. The thoracic duct is cut next to the tumor, and over the next days milky pleural fluid with a very high triglyceride level collects.
oneliner: 72F + posterior mediastinal mass surgery + thoracic duct cut + milky high-triglyceride pleural fluid → which structure loses its lymph drainage?
ask: Lymph return from which structure is most likely to be impaired?

options.C: Right side of the head and neck

whyNot.A: Right chest structures drain through right-sided trunks into the **right lymphatic duct**, not the thoracic duct
whyNot.B: The right arm drains via the right subclavian trunk to the **right lymphatic duct**
whyNot.C: The right jugular trunk joins the **right lymphatic duct**, not the **thoracic duct**
whyNot.D: The right breast drains via right axillary nodes to the **right lymphatic duct**

answer: Right kidney (all lymph from below the diaphragm drains by the thoracic duct)
why: The **thoracic duct** begins at the **cisterna chyli**, passes through the **aortic hiatus** and carries lymph from **everything below the diaphragm**, both sides, plus the **left side above it**. The **right lymphatic duct** drains only the right arm, right thorax and right head and neck, so the **right kidney** is the only listed structure that loses drainage. The **milky, triglyceride-rich fluid** is chyle.

idea.rule: Thoracic duct = all lymph below the diaphragm plus the left upper body; right lymphatic duct = right arm, right thorax, right head and neck.
also: Chyle is milky and rich in triglycerides from intestinal lymph
The duct crosses from right to left at about the T5 level
It empties at the left jugular-subclavian venous junction
A tear below T5 usually gives a right chylothorax and above T5 a left one

stem: An 82-year-old woman has a right pleural effusion that is dull to percussion from the 7th rib downward. She sits leaning forward on a bedside table, and a needle is to be passed through a posterior intercostal space below the dullness line.
oneliner: 82F + right pleural effusion dull below 7th rib + sitting leaning forward + posterior tap → where relative to the rib?
ask: How should the needle pass relative to the ribs bordering the space?

options.A: Along the upper edge of the rib below
options.B: Along the lower edge of the rib above
options.C: Through the outer surface of a rib
options.D: Through the middle of the space
options.E: Under the lower border of the rib below

whyNot.B: The **vein, artery and nerve** run in the groove under the **lower** border of that rib, so this edge risks **bleeding and pain**
whyNot.C: A needle cannot cross the **rib's bone**; it would be blocked and the rib hurt
whyNot.D: Mid-space is unsafe: the bundle and its **collateral branches** run close to the ribs, and only the **upper border of the lower rib** is reliably clear
whyNot.E: The lower border of the rib below hides the **costal groove** bundle of the next space down

answer: Just over the upper border of the rib below the space
why: Each intercostal **vein, artery and nerve (VAN)** lies in the **costal groove** under the **lower border** of the rib above. A thoracentesis needle therefore goes **just over the upper border of the rib below**, below the level of dullness, to avoid the bundle.

idea.rule: Go over the top of the rib; the neurovascular bundle hides under its lower edge.
also: Order from top to bottom is Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN)
Chest tubes are also inserted over the upper border of a rib
Pneumothorax is the commonest complication of thoracentesis
Injury to the intercostal artery can cause a hemothorax

stem: A 66-year-old woman has a large pleural effusion, and a needle is passed through the sixth intercostal space in the midaxillary line to drain it. Fluid lies between the lung and the chest wall.
oneliner: 66F + large pleural effusion + needle at sixth intercostal space, midaxillary line → which layers are crossed, in order?
ask: After the skin, which structures does the needle pierce, from superficial to deep?

whyNot.A: The visceral pleura covers the **lung surface**; the fluid lies **outside** it, so piercing it would puncture lung
whyNot.B: This skips the **muscle layer** and also pierces the **visceral pleura** on the lung surface
whyNot.D: The mediastinal pleura faces the **mediastinum**, medial to the site, not the **lateral chest wall**
whyNot.E: The order is reversed and the **visceral pleura** lies on the lung, deep to the fluid

why: Entering the pleural space from the lateral chest wall, the needle crosses the **intercostal muscles** and then the **costal (parietal) pleura**. It stops there, in the fluid; the **visceral pleura** stays on the lung and is not pierced.

idea.rule: A lateral chest tap crosses muscle and costal pleura; the visceral pleura stays on the lung.
also: The pleura reaches the 8th rib midclavicular, 10th midaxillary and 12th paravertebral
The lung reaches the 6th, 8th and 10th ribs at the same lines
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest point where fluid collects
The parietal pleura is pain-sensitive; the visceral pleura is not

stem: A 64-year-old man with lung cancer has bronchoscopy, and the bronchoscopist wants to take a lavage sample from the lingula.
oneliner: 64M + lung cancer + bronchoscopic lavage of the lingula → which bronchus does the scope pass on the way?
ask: Which bronchus must the scope enter on the way to the lingular bronchus?

whyNot.B: The left lower lobe bronchus supplies the **lower lobe**; the lingula belongs to the **upper lobe**
whyNot.C: The lingula is the left-sided counterpart of the middle lobe, but it is reached through the **left** bronchial tree
whyNot.D: The lingula is on the **left**, so the scope goes down the left main bronchus, not the right
whyNot.E: The basal segmental bronchi supply the **base of the lower lobe**, not the lingula of the **upper lobe**

answer: Left upper lobe bronchus (trachea, left main bronchus, then upper lobe)
why: The **lingula** is part of the **left upper lobe**, the left counterpart of the right middle lobe. The scope goes from the trachea into the **left main bronchus**, then the **left upper lobe bronchus**, which gives the superior and inferior lingular branches.

idea.rule: The lingula is part of the left upper lobe and the homolog of the right middle lobe.
also: The lingula has superior and inferior segments
The left lung has only an oblique fissure and no middle lobe
The lingula lies against the cardiac notch of the left lung
The right middle lobe is the right-sided homolog
